newsitem.title: INDIA: YEAREND - Indian grain output seen up, exports low.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Indian grain output seen up, exports low.

text.p: India expects to stage a sharp recovery in food grain production next year, but rice exports could be sluggish and international wheat sales are ruled out, traders and officials said on Thursday.
"The food grains situation will be comfortable, but I do not see much export prospect for wheat and rice," said Mulraj Tanna, a leading Bombay food grain exporter.
"There will be no wheat exports and rice exports will be limited to 1.5 to 2.0 million tonnes," he said.
Tanna said the government's priority was to build a food stocks buffer, provide low-priced essentials to the people, and hold inflationary pressures in check.
"The export scenario is sluggish unless you bring value addition like wheat flakes or corn flakes," said Rashmi Bhimjyani, another large exporter.
Last week, India decided to import two million tonnes of wheat in 1996/97 (April-March) to augment domestic supplies and check rising prices.
Dwindling government reserves have caused domestic wheat prices to rise sharply in recent months compared with last year. Traders said wheat prices has risen 40 percent in the last six months.
GOOD MONSOONS BOOST FOOD PRODUCTION

Agriculture Ministry officials said the outlook for food grain production in 1996/97 (July-June) was bright and output was likely to reach 197 million tonnes compared with 185 million tonnes in 1995/96.
They said this was primarly due to good rainfall distribution this year -- the best in the past five years.

India, predominantly an agricultural country, had its ninth good monsoon in a row in 1996. Agriculture employs about two-thirds of India's workers and accounts for more than a third of its gross domestic product (GDP).
High-yielding seeds, pesticides and credit facilities have helped India achieve self-sufficiency in agriculture since the 1970s, in what was called the "Green Revolution."
India's wheat procurement in 1995/96 dropped steeply to 8.2 million tonnes compared to 12.3 million tonnes the previous year, due to a three million-tonne shortfall in wheat output.
As of October 1, the Food Corporation of India (FCI) held 19.6 million tonnes of food grains -- wheat, rice and other cereals -- down from 29.9 million tonnes a year earlier.

The last time India imported more than two million tonnes of wheat was in 1992/93 (April-March). It exported 600,000 tonnes of the cereal in 1995/96 and 1.07 million tonnes up to September 30 this year, when the government halted exports.

India expects national wheat output to total nearly 66 million tonnes in 1996/97 and a clear picture of production trends will emerge by mid-January, when harvests begin in the western states of Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh.
India's northern states of Punjab, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh account for the bulk of the country's wheat output.
Bhimjyani said the government would not allow wheat exports next year in view of the depletion in stocks and to keep domestic prices under check.
INDIAN RICE EXPORTS SEEN AS UNCOMPETITIVE
Tanna said Indian rice export prices were not competitive compared to Vietnamese and Thai rice. "We are outpriced by $20 to $25 per tonne," he said.

Anil Adlakha, executive director of the All India Rice Exporters' Association, said Indian rice exports in 1996/97 were expected to be between 2.5 and 3.0 million tonnes, compared to more than five million tonnes in 1995/96.
He said Indian rice exports would drop due to a fall in world demand and good crops in Indonesia, Bangladesh and China.
Analysts said India had exported more thanr one million tonnes of wheat and continued to export rice, despite a fall in food grain output in 1995/96.
They said India had allowed imports of two million tonnes of wheat as a temporary measure, but actual arrivals might not exceed 500,000 tonnes.
Adlakha said India had 19 million hectares of arable land and private entrepreneurs were being encouraged to take up farming and to develop infrastructure and marketing to boost output.
